h: Why Board Games Never Really Go Out of Fashion
p: There's a reason board games keep coming back, generation after generation. They get people round a table, off their phones and talking to each other, and they carry memories in a way few other things do. The battered box with the sellotaped corners, the dog-eared rules nobody ever read properly, the house rule your uncle swore was official: every family has its own stories, and a visit to a museum devoted to games is a lovely way to swap them.

For children, it's a peek at how people played before screens took over. For parents and grandparents, it's a trip down memory lane that tends to start with a delighted "we had that one!" and end with a debate about who used to cheat. Even hardcore modern tabletop fans can get a kick out of seeing how game design has changed over the years, from simple roll-and-move classics to the heavy strategy titles of today.

Go in with time to chat rather than rushing round. Ask questions if there's someone on hand, because collectors and volunteers at specialist museums usually know the stories behind the pieces and love sharing them. Small venues can have limited space, so a pushchair might be trickier than in a big city museum, and a quick check before you go is wise.

Newent is a proper little market town, with a striking black-and-white timber-framed Market House in the centre that's well worth a photo. Just outside town, the International Centre for Birds of Prey is a natural pairing for families, and the Three Choirs Vineyard sits in the countryside nearby for grown-ups who fancy a glass with a view. Newent Lake, close to the centre, is a pleasant spot for a short stroll and a sit down after all that nostalgia.
